reading.p: Fog can come at any time, and visibility can fall away fast. Do not assume it will thin out once you are in it.

ul: Obey all fog warning signs.
Slow down BEFORE you enter the fog.
Use low-beam headlights and fog lights, even in daytime, and watch for drivers who forgot their lights.
Turn on your four-way flashers, so traffic behind sees you sooner.
Watch for vehicles stopped at the roadside. Taillights ahead may not show where the road goes: that vehicle may not be on the road at all.
Use the roadside reflectors to read the curve ahead.
Listen for traffic you cannot see.
Avoid passing.
Do not stop at the roadside unless you absolutely must.

reading.p: Winter needs a vehicle that is ready and a driver who slows down. Do your normal inspection, and give these items extra attention.

facts.text: Make sure the cooling system is full and has enough antifreeze to protect against freezing, which you check with a coolant tester.
Make sure the defrosters and heater work, and any mirror, battery box or fuel tank heaters you expect to need.
Wiper blades must press hard enough to wipe the windshield clean, or they will not sweep snow off.
Remove ice and snow from the windshield, windows and mirrors before starting, and from the hand holds, steps and deck plates so you do not slip.
Remove ice from the radiator shutters, and do not close the winterfront too tightly, or the engine may overheat and stop.
An exhaust leak is especially dangerous in winter, with the windows up: carbon monoxide makes you sleepy, and in large enough amounts it kills.

cards.q: Why is an exhaust leak so dangerous in winter?
cards.a: With the windows up, carbon monoxide builds in the cab. It makes you sleepy, and enough of it kills.

cards.q: Why clear the hand holds and steps?
cards.a: So you do not slip getting in and out.

cards.q: What happens if the winterfront is closed too tightly?
cards.a: The engine may overheat and stop.

exam.q: Why is a small exhaust leak worse in winter?
choices: Carbon monoxide collects in a closed cab
exam.why: With the windows up, carbon monoxide builds up. It makes you sleepy, and enough of it kills.

ul: Coolant level and antifreeze: full, and enough antifreeze to protect against freezing. Check it with a coolant tester.
Defrosters and heater working, plus any mirror, battery box or fuel tank heaters you will need.
Wipers and washers: blades in good condition, pressing hard enough to wipe clean, with fluid in the reservoir.
Windows and mirrors: clear all ice and snow before starting.
Hand holds, steps and deck plates: clear all ice and snow, so you do not slip.
Radiator shutters and winterfront: clear of ice, and not closed too tightly, or the engine may overheat and stop.

reading.note: Check the exhaust system for loose parts and signs of leaks. In winter the windows are up, and carbon monoxide collects in the cab. It makes you sleepy, and in large enough amounts it kills you.

facts.text: Drive slowly and smoothly on slippery roads. If it is very slippery, do not drive at all: stop at the first safe place.
A lack of spray from other vehicles means ice has formed on the road.
Ice on your mirrors or wiper blades means the road is probably icy too.
On slippery roads do not use the engine brake or the speed retarder: they can skid the driving wheels.
Take curves slower and do not brake in them. As the temperature rises and ice begins to melt, the road gets even more slippery, so slow down more.
Keep a longer following distance, do not drive alongside others, and give snowplows and salt and sand trucks plenty of room.
Water in the brakes makes them weak, uneven or grabbing, which can cause wheel lockups, pulling to one side, and a jackknife with a trailer.

To cross deep water: slow down into a low gear, put the brakes on gently to keep water out, raise the engine rpm, cross with light brake pressure, then keep light pressure a short way to heat and dry them, and make a test stop.
Do not apply heavy brake pressure and accelerator together: you can overheat the drums and linings.

cards.q: What does a lack of spray from other vehicles mean?
cards.a: Ice has formed on the road.

cards.q: Which brakes must you not use on slippery roads?
cards.a: The engine brake and the speed retarder: they skid the drive wheels.

cards.q: What do wet brakes do?
cards.a: They go weak, uneven or grabby, which can lock wheels, pull you sideways, or jackknife a trailer.

cards.q: How do you dry wet brakes?
cards.a: Keep light pressure on them for a short distance to heat them, then make a test stop.

cards.q: When is melting ice most dangerous?
cards.a: As the temperature rises to the melting point: the road becomes even more slippery.

exam.q: Other vehicles have stopped throwing spray on a wet road. What does that mean?
exam.why: A lack of spray means the water has frozen. The road is icy.

exam.q: You have driven through deep standing water. What now?
choices: Brake hard once to test them
Keep light pressure on the brakes to dry them, then test stop
exam.why: Light pressure heats and dries the brakes, then make a test stop when it is safe.

ul: Drive slowly and smoothly. If it is very slippery, do not drive at all: stop at the first safe place.
Start gently. Get the feel of the road before you hurry.
Check for ice, above all on bridges and overpasses. A LACK of spray from other vehicles means the road has iced. Ice on your mirrors or wiper blades says the same.
Turn as gently as you can. Brake no harder than you must. Do NOT use the engine brake or the retarder: they skid the drive wheels.
Take curves slower, and do not brake in them. As ice begins to melt the road gets MORE slippery, so slow down further.
Keep a longer following distance and do not drive alongside others. Give snowplows and salt and sand trucks plenty of room.

reading.p: Water in the brakes makes them weak, uneven, or grabbing, which can lock a wheel, pull you to one side, or jackknife a trailer. Avoid deep puddles and flowing water where you can. Where you cannot:

ul: Slow down and take a low gear.
Put the brakes on gently, which presses the linings against the drums and keeps water and grit out.
Raise the engine rpm and cross with light pressure on the brakes.
Out of the water, keep light pressure for a short distance to heat and dry them.
Make a test stop when it is safe, with nobody behind you.

reading.note: Do not apply heavy brake pressure and accelerator together, or you will overheat the drums and linings.

reading.p: Heat works on the tires, the oil, the coolant and the road surface. Do a normal inspection, with extra attention to these.

facts.text: In very hot weather, inspect the tires every two hours or every 100 miles.
Air pressure rises with temperature. Do NOT let air out of a hot tire, or the pressure will be too low when it cools.
If a tire is too hot to touch, stay stopped until it cools, or it may blow out or catch fire.
Engine oil cools as well as lubricates, so make sure there is enough, and watch the oil temperature gauge if you have one.
Never remove the radiator cap or any part of a pressurized system until it has cooled. Steam and boiling water spray out under pressure and cause severe burns.
If you can touch the radiator cap with a bare hand, it is probably cool enough to open.
To add coolant without a recovery tank: shut the engine off, let it cool, protect your hands, turn the cap slowly to the first stop to release pressure, step back, then press down and turn it off.
Loose belts will not turn the water pump or the fan properly, which causes overheating. Check belts for tightness, cracking and wear, and hoses for condition.

cards.q: How often do you check tires in very hot weather?
cards.a: Every two hours or every 100 miles.

cards.q: Should you let air out of a hot tire?
cards.a: No. The pressure will be too low when it cools.

cards.q: A tire is too hot to touch. What do you do?
cards.a: Stay stopped until it cools, or it may blow out or catch fire.

cards.q: When is it safe to open a radiator cap?
cards.a: Only when the system has cooled. If you can touch the cap bare-handed, it is probably cool enough.

exam.q: A tire is too hot to touch. What do you do?
exam.why: Remain stopped until it cools, or it may blow out or catch fire. Never let air out of a hot tire.

exam.q: How often should tires be checked in very hot weather?
exam.why: Every two hours or every 100 miles.

numbers.what: or every 100 miles: how often to inspect tires in very hot weather

reading.note: Air pressure rises with heat. Do NOT let air out of a hot tire, or it will be underinflated when it cools. If a tire is too hot to touch, stay stopped until it cools: it may blow out or catch fire.

ul: Engine oil cools as well as lubricates. Check there is enough, and watch the oil temperature gauge.
Coolant: enough water and antifreeze before you start, and watch the gauge as you drive. Above the highest safe temperature, stop as soon as it is safe and find out why.

reading.note: NEVER remove the radiator cap, or any part of a pressurized system, until it has cooled. Steam and boiling water spray out under pressure and cause severe burns. If you can touch the cap with a bare hand, it is probably cool enough.

reading.p: To add coolant with no recovery tank: engine off, let it cool, protect your hands, turn the cap slowly to the first stop to release the pressure, step back while it vents, then press down and turn it off.

Loose belts will not turn the water pump or fan properly, and the engine overheats. Check belt tightness, cracking and wear, and check the hoses: a hose that bursts while driving can mean engine failure or fire.

facts.text: Tar in the pavement rises to the surface in very hot weather, and the spots where it bleeds through are very slippery.
High speed makes more heat in the tires and the engine, which raises the chance of tire failure, fire and engine failure. Go slowly enough to prevent overheating.

cards.q: What is bleeding tar?
cards.a: Tar that rises to the road surface in hot weather. Those spots are very slippery.

ul: Watch for bleeding tar: in very hot weather tar rises to the surface, and those spots are very slippery.
Go slowly enough to prevent overheating. High speed builds heat in tires and engine, and in desert conditions that can mean tire failure, fire or engine failure.

facts.text: A railroad-highway grade crossing is a special kind of intersection, and every one of them must be approached expecting a train.
It is extremely difficult to judge both the distance and the speed of an approaching train.

cards.q: How should you approach every railroad crossing?
cards.a: Expecting a train. You cannot judge a train's distance or speed well.

reading.p: A grade crossing is an intersection where the road crosses the tracks. They are always dangerous.

reading.note: Approach EVERY crossing expecting a train. Judging the distance and the speed of an approaching train is extremely difficult, and people get both wrong.

facts.text: A passive crossing has no traffic control device. The decision to stop or go is entirely yours.
An active crossing has a control device: flashing red lights, with or without bells, or flashing red lights with bells and gates.

cards.q: What is a passive crossing?
cards.a: One with no traffic control device. The decision to stop or go is entirely yours.

ul: PASSIVE: no traffic control device at all. You must recognize the crossing, look for a train, and decide whether there is room to cross safely. The decision is entirely yours.
ACTIVE: a control device regulates the crossing. Flashing red lights, with or without bells, or flashing red lights with bells and gates.

facts.text: The advance warning sign is round and black on yellow. It means slow down, look and listen, and be ready to stop if a train is coming.
All passenger-carrying and hazmat-carrying vehicles are required to stop at a crossing.
Pavement markings mean the same as the advance warning sign: an X with the letters RR, and a no-passing marking on two-lane roads.
The cross-buck sign marks the crossing and requires you to yield the right of way to the train.
Where there is no white stop line, a vehicle required to stop must stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail.
A sign below the cross-buck gives the number of tracks when the road crosses more than one.
When the red lights begin to flash, stop. A train is coming, and you must yield the right of way. With gates, stop before the gate lowers and stay stopped until it rises and the lights stop flashing.

cards.q: What does the advance warning sign look like and mean?
cards.a: Round, black on yellow. Slow down, look and listen, and be ready to stop.

cards.q: Where must a vehicle required to stop actually stop?
cards.a: No closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail.

cards.q: What does a cross-buck require?
cards.a: Yielding the right of way to the train.

cards.q: Which vehicles must always stop at a crossing?
cards.a: Passenger-carrying and hazmat-carrying vehicles.

cards.q: When may you move off after the gates come down?
cards.a: Only when the gates go up and the lights stop flashing, and it is safe.

exam.q: With no stop line, where must a vehicle required to stop at a crossing stop?
choices: No closer than 15 feet, no more than 50
exam.why: No closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail.

exam.q: The advance warning sign for a crossing is:
exam.why: Round, black on yellow: slow down, look and listen, be ready to stop.

reading.p: Round, black on yellow, placed ahead of the crossing. Slow down, look and listen for a train, and be ready to stop at the tracks.

reading.note: All passenger-carrying and hazmat-carrying vehicles are REQUIRED to stop.

reading.p: An X with the letters RR, and a no-passing marking on two-lane roads. They mean the same as the advance warning sign. A white stop line may be painted before the tracks.
This marks the crossing itself and requires you to YIELD the right of way to the train. A sign below it gives the number of tracks when there is more than one.

numbers.what: the closest you may stop to the nearest rail
the farthest, where there is no white stop line

reading.p: When the lights begin to flash, STOP: a train is coming and you must yield. With more than one track, make sure all of them are clear. Where there are gates, stop before the gate lowers, and stay stopped until the gates go up and the lights stop flashing.

facts.text: Never race a train to a crossing. Judging the speed of an approaching train is extremely difficult.
Reduce speed to suit how far you can see along the track, and hold it to a point that lets you stop short of the tracks.
Do not expect to hear a train. Trains may not sound a horn at some crossings, and noise in your cab can hide it until the train is dangerously close.
Do not rely on signals, gates or flagmen alone, and be especially alert at crossings without gates or flashing lights.
A train on one track can hide a train on the other. Look both ways, and after one train has cleared, make sure no other is near before you start across.
Yard areas and crossings in cities and towns are just as dangerous as rural ones.

cards.q: Why is a double track especially dangerous?
cards.a: A train on one track can hide a train on the other. Look both ways, and again after one has passed.

cards.q: Can you rely on hearing a train?
cards.a: No. Trains may not sound a horn, and cab noise can hide it until the train is very close.

exam.q: A train has just cleared a double-track crossing. What now?
choices: Check that no other train is near on the second track
exam.why: A train on one track can hide one on the other. Look both ways before starting across.

ul: NEVER race a train to a crossing. You cannot judge its speed.
Reduce speed to suit how far you can see along the track, and keep it low enough to stop short of the rails.
Do not expect to HEAR a train. Some crossings prohibit horns, and cab noise can hide one until it is dangerously close.
Do not rely on signals, gates or flagmen. Be especially alert where there are none.
Double tracks need a double check: a train on one track can hide a train on the other. After one has cleared, look again before starting across.
Yard areas and crossings in cities and towns are just as dangerous as rural ones.

facts.text: A full stop is required whenever the cargo makes it mandatory under state or federal regulation, or the law otherwise requires it.
When stopping at a crossing, check the traffic behind you while slowing gradually, and use a pullout lane if there is one.
Turn on your four-way emergency flashers when you stop at a crossing.

cards.q: What must you switch on when stopping at a crossing?
cards.a: The four-way emergency flashers.

reading.p: A full stop is required whenever the cargo makes it mandatory under state or federal regulation, or the law otherwise requires it.

ul: Check the traffic behind you while you slow gradually.
Use a pullout lane if there is one.
Turn on your four-way emergency flashers.

facts.text: A crossing with steep approaches can hang your unit up on the tracks.
Never let traffic trap you where you must stop on the tracks. Be sure you can get ALL the way across before you start.
A typical tractor-trailer needs at least 14 seconds to clear a single track, and more than 15 seconds to clear a double track.
Do not shift gears while crossing railroad tracks.

cards.q: How long does a tractor-trailer need to clear a single track? A double?
cards.a: At least 14 seconds for a single, more than 15 for a double.

cards.q: May you shift gears on a crossing?
cards.a: No.

exam.q: How long does a typical tractor-trailer need to clear a single track?
exam.why: At least 14 seconds for a single track, more than 15 for a double.

exam.q: You are crossing the tracks and the engine is lugging. What do you do?
choices: Do not shift until you are fully across
exam.why: Never shift gears while crossing. Losing the gear could leave you stopped on the tracks.

numbers.what: at least, for a tractor-trailer to clear a SINGLE track
more than this, to clear a DOUBLE track

reading.note: Never let traffic conditions trap you where you must stop on the tracks. Be sure you can get ALL the way across before you start. And do NOT shift gears while crossing.

reading.p: A crossing with steep approaches can hang your unit up on the rails.

facts.text: Trailers that can get stuck on a raised crossing: low slung units such as a lowboy, car carrier, moving van or possum-belly livestock trailer, and a single-axle tractor pulling a long trailer whose landing gear is set for a tandem-axle tractor.
If you get stuck on the tracks, get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, then call 911 and give the crossing location with the DOT number if it is posted.

cards.q: Which trailers get stuck on raised crossings?
cards.a: Low slung ones: lowboy, car carrier, moving van, possum-belly livestock trailer.

cards.q: You are stuck on the tracks. What do you do?
cards.a: Get out and away from the tracks, then call 911 with the crossing's DOT number.

ul: Low slung units: a lowboy, a car carrier, a moving van, a possum-belly livestock trailer.
A single-axle tractor pulling a long trailer whose landing gear is set for a tandem-axle tractor.

reading.note: If you get stuck: get OUT of the vehicle and AWAY from the tracks. Find the emergency number on the signpost or signal housing, call 911, and give the location with the DOT crossing number if it is posted.

facts.text: Gravity slows you on an upgrade and speeds you on a downgrade. The steeper and longer the grade, and the heavier the load, the lower the gear you need.
Plan ahead and find out about long steep grades on your route, and ask drivers who know them what speeds are safe.
Go slowly enough that your brakes can hold you back without getting too hot. Too hot and they fade: you press harder and harder for the same stopping power, until they will not slow you at all.

cards.q: What is brake fade?
cards.a: Overheated brakes needing more and more pressure for the same stopping power, until they stop working.

reading.p: In the mountains gravity is the other driver. Going up it slows you, so you take lower gears. Coming down it speeds you, and your job is to hold the speed down without cooking the brakes.

reading.note: Go slowly enough that the brakes can hold you back without getting too hot. Overheated brakes FADE: you press harder and harder for the same effect, until they will not slow you at all.

reading.p: Plan ahead. Find out about the long steep grades on your route, and ask drivers who know them what speeds are safe.

facts.text: Choose a speed that suits the total weight of vehicle and cargo, the length of the grade, its steepness, the road conditions and the weather.
Never exceed a posted speed limit or a Maximum Safe Speed sign, and heed the signs giving the length and steepness of the grade.
Use the braking effect of the engine as your main way of controlling speed, saving the brakes to slow or stop as road and traffic require.

cards.q: What five things decide a safe downgrade speed?
cards.a: Total weight, length of grade, steepness, road conditions and weather.

ul: The total weight of the vehicle and cargo.
The length of the grade.
The steepness of the grade.
The road conditions.
The weather.

reading.note: Never exceed a posted limit or a Maximum Safe Speed sign. Use the ENGINE as the principal brake, and save the service brakes for slowing and stopping as the road and traffic require.

subsections.title: Select the Right Gear before Starting

facts.text: Shift to a low gear BEFORE starting down. Do not try to downshift after speed has built up: you may not get the lower gear, or any gear, and then all engine braking is lost.
Forcing an automatic into a lower gear at high speed can damage the transmission and lose all engine braking.
The old rule was to use the same gear down a hill as up it. A modern truck has lower friction, better streamlining and more power, so it may need a LOWER gear going down than going up.

cards.q: When do you select the gear for a downgrade?
cards.a: Before you start down. After speed builds you may not get any gear at all.

cards.q: Is the gear down the same as the gear up?
cards.a: That was the old rule. A modern truck may need a LOWER gear going down than going up.

exam.q: You are already rolling fast down a grade in too high a gear. What is likely?
choices: You may not get any gear, and lose all engine braking
exam.why: Downshifting after speed builds may leave you in no gear at all, with all engine braking gone.

reading.note: Shift to a low gear BEFORE you start down. Do not try to downshift once the speed has built up: you may not get the lower gear, and you may not get ANY gear, and then all engine braking is gone. Forcing an automatic down at speed can wreck the transmission and lose the braking too.

reading.p: The old rule was to use the same gear down a hill that you would need to climb it. Modern trucks have low friction parts, streamlined shapes and more powerful engines: they climb in higher gears and have less drag holding them back on the way down. So you may need a LOWER gear going down than going up. Know what is right for your vehicle.

facts.text: Brakes fade from the heat of using them too much instead of the engine's braking effect.
A brake out of adjustment stops doing its share, so the others overheat and fade, leaving too little braking to control the vehicle.
Brakes go out of adjustment quickly when used a lot, and linings wear faster when hot, so check the adjustment frequently.

cards.q: Why does one badly adjusted brake matter?
cards.a: It stops doing its share, so the others overheat and fade.

reading.p: Braking makes heat, and brakes are built to take a lot of it. But too much, from using them instead of the engine, and they fade.

reading.note: Every brake must do its share. A brake out of adjustment quits first, the others overheat and fade, and then there is not enough braking to control the vehicle. Brakes go out of adjustment quickly when worked hard, and hot linings wear faster, so check the adjustment often.

facts.text: Once in the proper low gear, apply the brakes just hard enough to feel a definite slowdown, then release when your speed is about five mph below your safe speed. The application lasts about three seconds.
Apply again when the speed returns to your safe speed, and repeat to the bottom. With a safe speed of 40 mph, brake at 40 down to 35, release, repeat.

cards.q: Describe proper downgrade braking.
cards.a: Brake to a definite slowdown, release about five mph below your safe speed, about three seconds each time, and repeat.

exam.q: Your safe speed is 40 mph on a downgrade. What is the braking pattern?
choices: Hold the brakes lightly all the way
Use the brakes only at corners
exam.why: Brake to a definite slowdown of about five mph, release, let it build back, repeat.

reading.note: The brakes only SUPPLEMENT the engine on a long or steep downgrade. Get into the proper low gear first.

ul: Apply the brakes just hard enough to feel a definite slowdown.
Release when your speed is about five mph below your safe speed. Each application lasts about three seconds.
Apply again when the speed comes back up to your safe speed.

reading.p: With a safe speed of 40 mph: brake at 40, slow to 35, release, and repeat to the bottom of the grade.
A traffic emergency is two vehicles about to collide. A vehicle emergency is a tire, a brake or another critical part failing. Whether you avoid the crash depends on what you do in the next second.

facts.text: You can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop. Stopping is not always the safest thing to do.
A top-heavy vehicle, or a tractor with multiple trailers, may flip over in a hard turn.
Keep both hands on the wheel all the time, because that is the only way to have them there when the emergency comes.
Do not brake while you are turning: it is very easy to lock the wheels and skid out of control.
Do not turn more than you need to clear the obstacle. The sharper the turn, the greater the chance of a skid or a rollover.
keywords: more than you need|no more than needed

facts.text: Be ready to counter-steer: turn back the other way once you have passed the obstacle. Think of the two turns as one action.
If an oncoming driver has drifted into your lane, move to your RIGHT, because their natural response is to return to their own lane.
If you are blocked on both sides, a move to the right is best: at least you do not force anyone into oncoming traffic and a head-on collision.
Leaving the road, avoid braking until your speed has dropped to about 20 mph, then brake gently to avoid skidding on the loose surface.
Keep one set of wheels on the pavement if you can, to help keep control, and stay on the shoulder until the vehicle has stopped.
Returning to the road before you can stop, hold the wheel tightly and turn sharply enough to get back on. Do not edge back gradually: the tires may grab and you lose control.
As soon as both front tires are on the pavement, counter-steer immediately. The two turns are one steer and counter-steer move.

cards.q: Can you stop faster than you can turn?
cards.a: No. You can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop.

cards.q: Which way do you go if an oncoming driver drifts into your lane?
cards.a: Right. Their natural response is to return to their own lane.

cards.q: Why not brake while turning hard?
cards.a: It is very easy to lock the wheels and skid out of control.

cards.q: When do you brake after leaving the road?
cards.a: Not until the speed is down to about 20 mph, then gently.

cards.q: How do you get back on the road from the shoulder?
cards.a: Hold the wheel tightly, turn sharply back on, then counter-steer the moment both front tires are on pavement.

exam.q: An oncoming vehicle has drifted into your lane. Which way do you steer?
exam.why: Move right: if they realize, their natural response is to return to their own lane.

exam.q: You are forced onto the shoulder at 55 mph. When do you brake?
choices: Once speed is down to about 20 mph
exam.why: Avoid braking until about 20 mph, then brake gently to avoid a skid on the loose surface.

reading.note: Stopping is not always safest. You can almost always TURN to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop. But a top-heavy vehicle, or a tractor with several trailers, may flip.

ul: Keep both hands on the wheel all the time, so they are there when you need them.
Do NOT brake while turning. The wheels lock easily and you skid.
Do not turn more than you need to clear the obstacle.
Be ready to COUNTER-STEER back the other way once you are past. Think of the turn and the counter-steer as one action.
Oncoming driver drifting into your lane: go RIGHT. Their natural response is to return to their own lane.
Something blocking your path: the mirrors tell you which lane is empty.
The shoulder is usually clear: nobody drives there, while someone may be passing on your left.
Blocked both sides: right is best. At least you force nobody into oncoming traffic.

reading.h: Leaving and returning to the road

ul: Most shoulders will carry a large vehicle, so they are a real escape route.
Avoid braking until your speed is down to about 20 mph, then brake gently.
Keep one set of wheels on the pavement if you can.
Stay on the shoulder until you stop. Signal and check mirrors before pulling back on.
If you must return before stopping, hold the wheel tightly and turn sharply enough to get back on. Do NOT edge back gradually: the tires can grab and you lose control.
The instant both front tires are on pavement, counter-steer.

subsections.title: How to Stop Quickly and Safely

facts.text: Brake so the vehicle stays in a straight line and you can still turn. Use controlled braking or stab braking.
Controlled braking: brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels, with very small steering movements. Release if a wheel locks or you need to steer more, then re-apply.
Stab braking: apply fully, release when the wheels lock, apply fully again when they start rolling. It can take up to a second for them to roll again.
Do not jam the brakes on. Emergency braking is not pushing as hard as you can: that locks the wheels, and a skidding vehicle cannot be controlled.

cards.q: What are the two emergency braking methods?
cards.a: Controlled braking and stab braking.

cards.q: Is emergency braking the same as stamping on the pedal?
cards.a: No. Jamming the brakes locks the wheels, and a skidding vehicle cannot be controlled.

exam.q: What is wrong with jamming the brake pedal down in an emergency?
choices: It locks the wheels and you lose control
It is only wrong with ABS
exam.why: Locked wheels mean a skid, and a skidding vehicle cannot be steered.

reading.p: Braking is the right answer when you have room to stop and you brake properly. Brake so the vehicle stays in a straight line and you can still turn.

ul: Brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels.
Keep steering movements very small.
If a wheel locks, or you need to steer more, release and re-apply as soon as you can.
Apply the brakes all the way.
Release when the wheels lock.
Apply fully again as soon as the wheels start rolling: it can take up to a second.

reading.note: Do NOT jam the brakes on. Emergency braking is not pushing as hard as you can. That keeps the wheels locked, and a skidding vehicle cannot be controlled.

facts.text: Most hydraulic brake failures come from loss of hydraulic pressure, or brake fade on long hills.
With no pressure the pedal feels spongy or goes to the floor. Downshift, pump the pedal, and use the parking brake.

The parking or emergency brake is separate from the hydraulic system, so it can slow you. Hold the release button or lever as you use it, so you can adjust the pressure and keep the wheels from locking.
Look for an escape route: an open field, a side street, or an escape ramp. Turning uphill is a good way to slow and stop.
After stopping uphill, keep the vehicle from rolling back: low gear, parking brake, and if necessary roll back into something that will stop it.
Escape ramps are usually a few miles from the top of a downgrade, and signs tell you about them. Use one if your brakes fail.
If there is no escape ramp, take the least hazardous route you can, and move as soon as you know the brakes have gone. The longer you wait the faster you go.

cards.q: What are the two main causes of hydraulic brake failure?
cards.a: Loss of hydraulic pressure, and brake fade on long hills.

cards.q: The pedal goes to the floor. What do you do?
cards.a: Downshift, pump the pedal, use the parking brake, and look for an escape route.

cards.q: What is an escape ramp?
cards.a: A ramp a few miles below the top of a grade, with soft gravel or an uphill slope, to stop a runaway.

cards.q: Why hold the release while using the parking brake to stop?
cards.a: So you can adjust the pressure and keep the wheels from locking.

exam.q: Your brakes fail on a downgrade and there is an escape ramp ahead. What do you do?
choices: Pass it and try the next exit
Use it only if you cannot slow down
exam.why: Use the ramp. Hundreds of drivers a year avoid injury that way.

reading.p: Brakes in good condition rarely fail. Hydraulic failures come from two things: loss of hydraulic pressure, and brake fade on a long hill.
The pedal feels spongy or goes to the floor.

ul: DOWNSHIFT into a lower gear to slow the vehicle.
PUMP the pedal: sometimes that builds enough pressure to stop.
Use the PARKING BRAKE, which is separate from the hydraulic system. Hold the release button or lever as you apply it, so you can adjust the pressure and keep the wheels from locking.
Find an ESCAPE ROUTE: an open field, a side street, an escape ramp. Turning uphill slows and stops you well.

reading.note: After stopping uphill, do not let it roll back: low gear, parking brake, and if you must, roll back into something that will hold it.

reading.p: Once the brakes are gone you must look outside the vehicle for something to stop it. Your best hope is an escape ramp, usually a few miles from the top, with signs to warn you. Some use soft gravel, some turn uphill.

reading.note: If you lose your brakes going downhill, USE the escape ramp. If there is none, take the least hazardous route you can find, and move as soon as you know. The longer you wait, the faster you go and the harder it gets.

facts.text: Signs of tire failure: the loud bang of a blowout, heavy thumping or vibration, and steering that feels heavy.
Heavy steering usually means a FRONT tire has failed. A rear tire failure may show only as vibration, or a fishtail.
Any time you hear a tire blow, assume it is yours.
Hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands: a failed front tire can twist the wheel out of your hands.
Stay OFF the brake. Braking with a failed tire can cost you control. Unless you are about to hit something, wait until the vehicle slows, then brake very gently and pull off.
After stopping, get out and check all the tires, even if it felt fine. A failed dual may only be found by looking.

cards.q: What does heavy steering mean?
cards.a: A front tire has probably failed.

cards.q: A tire blows. Do you brake?
cards.a: No. Stay off the brake until the vehicle slows, then brake very gently and pull off.

cards.q: Why check all the tires after a blowout?
cards.a: A failed dual may show no symptoms. The only way to know is to look.

exam.q: A tire blows out at speed. What do you do first?
choices: Hold the wheel firmly and stay off the brake
Steer for the shoulder at once
exam.why: Grip the wheel with both hands and stay off the brake until the vehicle slows.

ul: SOUND: the loud bang of a blowout. It may take seconds for the vehicle to react, so any time you hear a tire blow, assume it is yours.
VIBRATION: heavy thumping may be the only sign of a rear tire going flat.
FEEL: heavy steering usually means a FRONT tire has failed. A rear failure may fishtail the vehicle, though duals usually prevent it.
Hold the wheel FIRMLY with both hands. A front tire failure can twist it out of your grip.
STAY OFF THE BRAKE. Braking now can cost you control. Unless you are about to hit something, wait for the vehicle to slow, then brake very gently and pull off.
Once stopped, get out and check ALL the tires. A failed dual may show nothing from the seat.

reading.p: Section 5 covers air brake ABS in detail. These are the points every driver needs, whatever the brake system.

facts.text: Sensors detect a wheel about to lock, and an electronic control unit reduces brake pressure to prevent it, adjusting for maximum braking without lockup.
ABS works far faster than a driver can respond. At all other times the brakes work normally.

cards.q: How does ABS work?
cards.a: Sensors detect an impending lockup and the control unit reduces brake pressure, far faster than a driver could.

ul: Sensors detect a wheel about to lock.
An electronic control unit reduces the brake pressure to prevent it.
The pressure is adjusted for maximum braking without lockup.
It works far faster than a driver can respond. The rest of the time the brakes work normally.

facts.text: ABS is required on truck tractors with air brakes built on or after 1 March 1997.
ABS is required on other air brake vehicles, trucks, buses, trailers and converter dollies, built on or after 1 March 1998.
ABS is required on hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a gross vehicle weight rating of 10,000 pounds or more built on or after 1 March 1999.

cards.q: Which three ABS dates must you know?
cards.a: Air brake tractors 1 March 1997, other air brake vehicles 1 March 1998, hydraulic trucks and buses over 10,000 lb 1 March 1999.

exam.q: Hydraulically braked trucks over 10,000 lb need ABS if built on or after:
exam.why: 1999 for hydraulic. 1997 for air brake tractors, 1998 for other air brake vehicles.

numbers.what: truck tractors with air brakes
other air brake vehicles: trucks, buses, trailers, converter dollies
hydraulically braked trucks and buses of 10,000 lb GVWR or more

reading.p: Many vehicles built before those dates were given ABS anyway.

subsections.title: How to Know If Your Vehicle Is

facts.text: Tractors, trucks and buses carry a yellow ABS malfunction lamp on the instrument panel. Trailers carry one on the left side, front or rear corner.
The lamp comes on at start-up for a bulb check and goes out. On an older system it may stay on until you are over five mph.
If the lamp stays on after the bulb check, or comes on while driving, you may have lost ABS control.

cards.q: Where is the ABS lamp on a trailer?
cards.a: On the left side, at the front or rear corner. It is yellow.

ul: Tractors, trucks and buses: a yellow lamp on the instrument panel.
Trailers: a yellow lamp on the LEFT side, front or rear corner.
It lights at start-up for a bulb check then goes out. On older systems it may stay on until over five mph.
If it stays on after the bulb check, or comes on while you drive, you may have lost ABS at one or more wheels.
On an older towed unit, look underneath for the control unit and wheel speed sensor wires.

facts.text: Without ABS, hard braking on a slippery surface can lock the wheels: locked steering wheels take away steering, and other locked wheels skid, jackknife or spin the vehicle.
With ABS you may or may not stop faster, but you should be able to steer round an obstacle while braking.

cards.q: What does ABS let you do while braking hard?
cards.a: Steer around an obstacle, instead of skidding straight on.

reading.p: Brake hard on a slippery road without ABS and the wheels lock. Locked steering wheels mean no steering. Other locked wheels mean a skid, a jackknife or a spin.

reading.note: With ABS you may or may not stop faster, but you should be able to STEER around an obstacle while braking, and avoid skids from over-braking.

subsections.title: ABS on the Tractor Only or Only on the Trailer

facts.text: ABS on only the tractor, only the trailer, or even one axle still gives more control. Brake normally.
With ABS on the tractor only, you should keep steering control and a jackknife is less likely, but watch the trailer and ease off the brakes if it swings out.
With ABS on the trailer only, the trailer is less likely to swing out, but ease off the brakes if you lose steering or start a tractor jackknife.

cards.q: Only one unit has ABS. How do you brake?
cards.a: Normally. It still gives more control, whichever unit has it.

ul: ABS on only the tractor, only the trailer, or even one axle, still gives more control. Brake normally.
Tractor only: you should keep steering control, with less chance of a jackknife. Watch the trailer and ease off if it swings out.
Trailer only: the trailer is less likely to swing out, but ease off if you lose steering or start a tractor jackknife.

facts.text: Brake as you always have: use only the force you need to stop safely and stay in control, whichever units have ABS.
The one exception: with working ABS on ALL axles, you may fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop.

cards.q: When may you fully apply the brakes?
cards.a: Only in an emergency, in a vehicle with working ABS on all axles.

ul: Use only the braking force you need to stop safely and stay in control.
Brake the same way whether the ABS is on the bus, the tractor, the trailer or all of them.
As you slow, watch the units and back off the brakes, if safe, to stay in control.

reading.note: One exception only: with working ABS on ALL axles, you may fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop.

subsections.title: Braking If ABS Is Not Working

facts.text: If the ABS fails you still have normal brakes. Drive and brake as you always have, and get the system serviced soon.

cards.q: Your ABS fails. What brakes do you have?
cards.a: Your normal brakes. Drive normally and get it serviced soon.

reading.p: Without ABS you still have normal brake functions. Drive and brake as you always have, and get the system serviced soon.

facts.text: ABS will not let you drive faster, follow more closely, or drive less carefully.
ABS will not prevent a power skid or a turning skid. It prevents brake-induced skids and jackknifes, not skids from spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn.
ABS will not necessarily shorten the stopping distance, and it does not increase or decrease your ultimate stopping power: it is an add-on, not a replacement.
ABS will not compensate for bad brakes or poor maintenance.
The best vehicle safety feature is still a safe driver. Drive so you never need the ABS.

cards.q: Will ABS prevent a skid from going too fast in a turn?
cards.a: No. It prevents brake-induced skids, not power or turning skids.

cards.q: What is the best vehicle safety feature?
cards.a: A safe driver. Drive so you never need the ABS.

exam.q: Which skid will ABS NOT prevent?
choices: A skid from going too fast in a turn
A lockup on ice under braking
exam.why: ABS prevents brake-induced skids. It cannot help a power skid or a turning skid.

ul: It will not let you drive faster, follow more closely, or drive less carefully.
It will not prevent a power skid or a turning skid. It handles skids and jackknifes caused by BRAKING, not by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn.
It will not necessarily shorten your stopping distance.
It will not increase or decrease your ultimate stopping power. It is an add-on, not a replacement.
It will not change how you normally brake.
It will not make up for bad brakes or poor maintenance.

reading.note: The best vehicle safety feature is still a safe driver. Drive so you never need the ABS. But if you do need it, it may prevent a serious crash.

facts.text: A skid happens when the tires lose their grip, from one of four causes: over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, or driving too fast.
Most serious skids come from driving too fast for the conditions.
A skid can also come from using the speed retarder when the road is slippery.

cards.q: What are the four causes of a skid?
cards.a: Over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, and driving too fast.

cards.q: What causes most serious skids?
cards.a: Driving too fast for the conditions.

exam.q: What causes most serious skids?
exam.why: Drivers who adjust to conditions do not have to over-brake or over-steer.

reading.p: A skid is simply the tires losing their grip. There are four ways to cause one.

ul: OVER-BRAKING: braking too hard and locking the wheels. Also using the retarder on a slippery road.
OVER-STEERING: turning the wheels more sharply than the vehicle can turn.
OVER-ACCELERATION: too much power to the drive wheels, which spin.
DRIVING TOO FAST: most serious skids come from this. A driver who adjusts to the conditions does not have to over-brake or over-steer.

facts.text: The most common skid by far is the rear wheels losing traction through too much braking or acceleration.
An acceleration skid usually happens on ice or snow, and taking your foot off the accelerator stops it. If it is very slippery, push the clutch in too.

In a rear wheel braking skid the locked rear wheels slide sideways to catch up with the front. A straight truck or bus spins out; with a trailer, the trailer pushes the tractor sideways into a sudden jackknife.

cards.q: What is the most common kind of skid?
cards.a: The rear wheels losing traction from too much braking or acceleration.

cards.q: How do you stop an acceleration skid?
cards.a: Take your foot off the accelerator. If it is very slippery, push the clutch in too.

reading.p: By far the most common skid is the rear wheels losing traction, through too much braking or too much acceleration.

ul: Acceleration skids usually happen on ice or snow. Take your foot off the accelerator. If it is very slippery, push the clutch in as well, or the engine will keep the wheels from rolling freely and regaining traction.

In a braking skid the locked rear wheels slide sideways, trying to catch up with the front. A bus or straight truck spins out. With a trailer, the trailer pushes the towing vehicle sideways into a sudden jackknife.

facts.text: To correct a drive-wheel braking skid, STOP BRAKING. That lets the rear wheels roll again and stops them sliding.
Then counter-steer. As the vehicle comes back on course it tends to keep turning, so you must turn the wheel quickly the other way or you will skid in the opposite direction.
Staying off the brake, turning quickly, pushing in the clutch and counter-steering takes practice, best done on a driving range or skid pad.

cards.q: How do you correct a drive-wheel braking skid?
cards.a: Stop braking, then counter-steer quickly as it comes back on course.

cards.q: Why counter-steer?
cards.a: The vehicle keeps turning as it comes back, so without it you skid the other way.

exam.q: Your drive wheels have locked and the rear is sliding. What is the first action?
exam.why: Release the brakes so the rear wheels roll again, then counter-steer.

ul: STOP BRAKING. That lets the rear wheels roll again and stops the slide.
COUNTER-STEER. As the vehicle comes back on course it tends to keep turning, so turn the wheel quickly the other way, or you will skid in the opposite direction.

reading.note: Staying off the brake, turning quickly, pushing in the clutch and counter-steering all at once takes practice. A large driving range or a skid pad is the place to get it.

facts.text: Most front-wheel skids come from driving too fast for conditions. Other causes are a lack of tread on the front tires, and cargo loaded so there is too little weight on the front axle.
In a front-wheel skid the front end goes straight on however much you turn the wheel, and on a very slippery surface you may not be able to steer round a curve at all.
The only way to stop a front-wheel skid is to let the vehicle slow down: stop turning and braking so hard, and slow as quickly as you can without skidding.

cards.q: What causes most front-wheel skids?
cards.a: Driving too fast for conditions, plus worn front tread and too little weight on the front axle.

cards.q: How do you stop a front-wheel skid?
cards.a: Let the vehicle slow: stop turning and braking so hard.

exam.q: In a front-wheel skid, what is the only cure?
exam.why: Stop turning and braking so hard and let it slow. Steering more does nothing: the front end goes straight on.

reading.p: In a front-wheel skid the front end goes straight on, however much you turn the wheel. On a very slippery surface you may not be able to steer round a curve or turn at all.

ul: Driving too fast for conditions, which causes most of them.
A lack of tread on the front tires.
Cargo loaded so there is too little weight on the front axle.

reading.note: The ONLY way to stop a front-wheel skid is to let the vehicle slow down. Stop turning and braking so hard, and slow as quickly as you can without skidding.

facts.text: The three basic steps at any accident are: protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured.

cards.q: What are the three steps at an accident?
cards.a: Protect the area, notify the authorities, care for the injured.

exam.q: What are the basic steps at an accident scene, in order?
choices: Protect the area, notify authorities, care for the injured
exam.why: Protect the area first, so no second crash happens in the same spot.

reading.p: When you are in an accident and not seriously hurt, you must act to prevent further damage or injury.

ul: Protect the area.
Notify the authorities.
Care for the injured.

facts.text: The first thing at a scene is to keep a second accident from happening in the same spot.
If your vehicle is involved, try to get it to the side of the road, which prevents another accident and lets traffic move.

cards.q: What is the first thing to do at an accident?
cards.a: Stop another accident happening in the same place.

reading.p: The first job is to stop a second accident happening in the same spot.

ul: If your vehicle is in the accident, try to get it to the side of the road.
If you are stopping to help, park well clear of the scene.
Put on the four-way flashers and set out warning devices.

facts.text: Notify the authorities, giving the location and what has happened, before you do anything else that can wait.

reading.p: Call the authorities. Give the location and what has happened. If you can send somebody else to call while you protect the scene, do that.

facts.text: Do not move a badly injured person unless the danger of fire or passing traffic makes it necessary.
Stop heavy bleeding with direct pressure on the wound, and keep the injured person warm.

cards.q: How do you stop heavy bleeding?
cards.a: Direct pressure on the wound. Then keep the person warm.

cards.q: When do you move an injured person?
cards.a: Only when fire or passing traffic makes it necessary.

exam.q: Someone is badly injured in a crash. When should you move them?
choices: Only if fire or traffic makes it necessary
exam.why: Moving a badly injured person can do more harm. Move them only when the danger demands it.

ul: Do not move a badly injured person unless the danger of fire or passing traffic makes it necessary.
Stop heavy bleeding with direct pressure on the wound.
Keep the injured person warm.

reading.p: Truck fires cause damage and injury, and drivers who did not know what to do have made them worse. Learn the causes, the prevention, and the extinguisher.

facts.text: After an accident, spilled fuel and the improper use of flares cause fires.
Tires cause fires when they are under-inflated or when duals touch each other.
The electrical system causes fires through short circuits from damaged insulation and loose connections.
Fuel causes fires through driver smoking, improper fueling and loose fuel connections.
Cargo causes fires when it is flammable, improperly sealed or loaded, or poorly ventilated.

cards.q: Name two causes of tire fires.
cards.a: Under-inflated tires, and duals that touch each other.

cards.q: Name the five sources of vehicle fires.
cards.a: After accidents, tires, the electrical system, fuel, and cargo.

exam.q: Which two tire conditions cause fires?
exam.why: Under-inflated tires and duals that touch each other.

ul: AFTER ACCIDENTS: spilled fuel, improper use of flares.
TIRES: under-inflated tires, and duals that touch.
ELECTRICAL SYSTEM: short circuits from damaged insulation and loose connections.
FUEL: driver smoking, improper fueling, loose fuel connections.
CARGO: flammable cargo, improperly sealed or loaded cargo, poor ventilation.

facts.text: Inspect the electrical, fuel and exhaust systems, the tires and the cargo, and check the fire extinguisher is charged.
At every stop on a trip, check the tires, wheels and truck body for signs of heat.
Check the instruments and gauges often for overheating, and use the mirrors to look for smoke from the tires or the vehicle.

cards.q: What do you check at each stop to prevent fire?
cards.a: The tires, wheels and body for signs of heat.

ul: Inspection: the electrical, fuel and exhaust systems, the tires, the cargo, and a charged fire extinguisher.
En route: check the tires, wheels and body for signs of heat at every stop.
Follow safe procedures for fueling, braking and handling flares.
Monitor the instruments for overheating, and use the mirrors to look for smoke.
Handle anything flammable with normal caution.

facts.text: Pull off the road and park in an open area away from buildings, trees, brush and other vehicles. Do NOT pull into a service station.
Notify emergency services of the problem and your location.
With an engine fire, turn the engine off as soon as you can, and do not open the hood if you can avoid it. Shoot foam through the louvers, the radiator or from underneath.
With a cargo fire in a van or box trailer, keep the doors SHUT. Opening them feeds the fire oxygen and it will burn very fast.
Stay as far away from the fire as you can, and aim at the source or base of the fire, not up in the flames.
A B:C extinguisher works on electrical fires and burning liquids. An A:B:C also works on burning wood, paper and cloth.
Never use water on an electrical fire, because of shock, or on a gasoline fire, because it spreads the flames.
A burning tire must be cooled, and that can take a great deal of water.
Position yourself upwind, so the wind carries the extinguisher to the fire, and keep going until everything that burned has cooled. No smoke or flame does not mean it cannot restart.
If you are not sure what to use, above all on a hazardous materials fire, wait for the firefighters.

cards.q: Where do you stop with a fire aboard?
cards.a: In an open area away from buildings, trees and other vehicles. Never a service station.

cards.q: Cargo fire in a van. Do you open the doors?
cards.a: No. Keep them shut. Opening them feeds the fire oxygen.

cards.q: Where do you aim an extinguisher?
cards.a: At the source or base of the fire, not up in the flames, from as far away as you can.

cards.q: What is a B:C extinguisher for? An A:B:C?
cards.a: B:C for electrical fires and burning liquids. A:B:C adds wood, paper and cloth.

cards.q: When must you never use water?
cards.a: On an electrical fire, because of shock, and on a gasoline fire, because it spreads the flames.

cards.q: Which way should you stand to use an extinguisher?
cards.a: Upwind, so the wind carries it to the fire.

exam.q: Your cargo is on fire in a box trailer. What do you do with the doors?
choices: Open them to fight the fire
exam.why: Opening the doors gives the fire oxygen and it burns very fast. Keep them shut.

exam.q: Where do you aim a fire extinguisher?
choices: At the top of the flames
At the base or source of the fire
exam.why: Aim at the source or base, from as far away as you can, standing upwind.

exam.q: Which fire must you never fight with water?
exam.why: Water on an electrical fire can shock you, and on a gasoline fire it spreads the flames.

ul: Park in an OPEN area, away from buildings, trees, brush and other vehicles.
Do NOT pull into a service station.
Notify emergency services of the problem and your location.
Engine fire: turn the engine off as soon as you can. Do not open the hood if you can avoid it. Shoot foam through the louvers, the radiator, or from underneath.
Cargo fire in a van or box trailer: keep the doors SHUT, above all with hazardous materials aboard. Opening them feeds the fire oxygen and it burns very fast.
Stay as far from the fire as you can.
Aim at the SOURCE or BASE of the fire, not up in the flames.
Stand upwind, and let the wind carry the extinguisher to the fire.
Keep going until everything that burned has COOLED. No smoke and no flame does not mean it cannot restart.

numbers.what: electrical fires and burning liquids
those, plus burning wood, paper and cloth

reading.note: Never use water on an ELECTRICAL fire: it can shock you. Never on a GASOLINE fire: it spreads the flames. A burning tire must be cooled, and that takes a lot of water. If you are not sure what to use, above all on a hazardous materials fire, wait for the firefighters.

reading.p: Alcohol and other drugs behind the wheel end driving careers and lives. These are the facts the test asks for.

facts.text: People who drink alcohol are involved in traffic accidents causing over 20,000 deaths every year.
Alcohol impairs muscle coordination, reaction time, depth perception and night vision, and it affects the parts of the brain that control judgment and inhibition.
The liver can only process about one third of an ounce of alcohol an hour, less than one standard drink. The rate is fixed, so only TIME sobers you up: not coffee, not a cold shower.
These contain the same amount of alcohol: a 12 ounce glass of 5 percent beer, a 5 ounce glass of 12 percent wine, and a 1.5 ounce shot of 80 proof liquor.
Blood alcohol concentration depends on how much you drink, how fast you drink it, and your weight.
The FIRST part of the brain affected is the part controlling judgment and self-control, which is why a drinker may not know they are getting drunk.
Alcohol shows in driving as straddling lanes, quick jerky starts, not signaling, running stop signs and lights, improper passing, weaving and wrong-lane driving.

cards.q: How fast can the liver process alcohol?
cards.a: About one third of an ounce an hour, less than one standard drink. The rate is fixed.

cards.q: What sobers a person up?
cards.a: Only time. Not coffee, not a cold shower.

cards.q: What three things determine BAC?
cards.a: How much you drink, how fast, and your weight.

cards.q: Which part of the brain goes first?
cards.a: The part controlling judgment and self-control, which is why drinkers do not notice.

cards.q: What counts as one drink?
cards.a: 12 oz of 5% beer, 5 oz of 12% wine, or 1.5 oz of 80 proof liquor. All the same alcohol.

exam.q: What will sober up a person who has drunk too much?
exam.why: The liver works at a fixed rate, about a third of an ounce an hour. Only time.

exam.q: Which part of the brain does alcohol affect first?
exam.why: Judgment and self-control go first, which is why drinkers do not realize they are impaired.

numbers.what: deaths a year in accidents involving drinking drivers
the alcohol your liver can process in an hour: less than one drink

numbers.value: 12 oz beer at 5% = 5 oz wine at 12% = 1.5 oz of 80 proof
numbers.what: the same amount of alcohol in each

reading.note: The rate is FIXED. Only time sobers you up. Not black coffee, not a cold shower.

reading.p: Alcohol impairs muscle coordination, reaction time, depth perception and night vision. Your BAC depends on how much you drink, how fast you drink it, and your weight.

reading.note: The FIRST part of the brain affected is the part that controls judgment and self-control. That is why a drinker often cannot tell they are getting drunk, and judgment is exactly what safe driving needs.

reading.p: It shows in the driving: straddling lanes, quick jerky starts, no signals, running stop signs and lights, improper passing, weaving, driving too fast or too slow, running over the curb.

facts.text: The law prohibits possession or use of many drugs on duty, and being under the influence of any controlled substance, amphetamine, narcotic or other substance that makes a driver unsafe.
That can include prescription and over-the-counter drugs, such as cold medicines, which make a driver drowsy.
A drug given by a doctor is permitted if the doctor tells the driver it will not affect safe driving ability.
Do not use any drug that hides fatigue: the only cure for fatigue is rest. Alcohol makes the effects of other drugs much worse.

cards.q: When is a prescribed drug allowed?
cards.a: When the doctor says it will not affect your safe driving ability.

cards.q: What is the only cure for fatigue?
cards.a: Rest. Never a drug that hides it.

exam.q: Your doctor prescribes a medicine. When may you drive on it?
choices: Only if the doctor says it will not affect safe driving
exam.why: A doctor's drug is permitted if the doctor informs you it will not affect your safe driving ability.

reading.p: Laws prohibit possession or use of many drugs on duty, and being under the influence of any controlled substance, amphetamine, narcotic or anything else that makes a driver unsafe. That can include prescription and over-the-counter medicines, such as cold tablets, which make you drowsy.

reading.note: A drug given by a doctor is permitted IF the doctor tells you it will not affect your safe driving ability. Read the warning labels, and follow the doctor's orders.

reading.p: Do not use any drug that hides fatigue: the only cure for fatigue is rest. Alcohol makes other drugs much worse. The safest rule is not to mix drugs with driving at all.

facts.text: If you are so ill that you cannot drive safely, you must not drive. In an emergency you may drive to the nearest place where you can safely stop.

cards.q: You fall ill and cannot drive safely. What does the rule allow?
cards.a: You must not drive, except in an emergency, to the nearest place you can safely stop.

reading.p: Once in a while you may be so ill that you cannot drive safely. Then you must not drive.

reading.note: The one exception: in an emergency you may drive to the nearest place where you can safely stop.

subsections.title: Hazardous Materials Rules For All Commercial Drivers

reading.p: Every driver must be able to recognize hazardous cargo, and know whether they may haul it without a hazardous materials endorsement.

facts.text: Hazardous materials are products that pose a risk to health, safety and property during transportation.

cards.q: What are hazardous materials?
cards.a: Products that pose a risk to health, safety and property during transportation.

reading.p: Hazardous materials are products that pose a risk to health, safety and property during transportation.

facts.text: The hazmat rules have three intents: contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment.
The shipper communicates the risk with a shipping paper and diamond shaped hazard labels.
After a crash or a spill you may be injured and unable to speak, so firefighters and police must find the papers fast. Identify the hazmat shipping papers, or keep them on top of the others.

facts.text: Placards are signs on the outside of the vehicle that identify the hazard class of the cargo.
A placarded vehicle must have at least four identical placards: front, rear and both sides, readable from all four directions.
Placards must be at least 9.84 inches, which is 250 millimeters, square, turned upright on a point in a diamond shape.
Identification numbers are a four digit code used by first responders, preceded by the letters NA or UN, and listed in the Emergency Response Guidebook.
You may drive a vehicle carrying hazardous materials that does NOT require placards. If it requires placards, you may not drive it without the hazardous materials endorsement.
